skill.name: git-workflow
skill.description: Guides Git worktree use, conventional commit messages, commit trailers, pull request descriptions, and review checklists.
skill.summary: Standardizes Git worktrees, commits, trailers, and pull requests for team development.
skill.author: Cain96

security_audit.summary: The static findings are documentation examples in SKILL.md, not executable skill code or malicious instructions. Git commands, sibling worktree paths, and the Conventional Commits link match the stated purpose of Git workflow guidance. No prompt injection, credential theft, data exfiltration, or unauthorized network behavior was found.

remediation.issue: Destructive Git cleanup examples can be copied without context.
remediation.suggestion: Add a note to confirm the current repository, target path, and user intent before running worktree removal commands.

static_findings.snippet: | `fix` | Bug fix | Fixing null pointer error |
| `style` | Formatting changes | Code formatting, no logic change |
| `refactor` | Code refactoring | Restructure without behavior change |
| `build` | Build system changes | Update webpack config |
| `revert` | Revert previous commit | Revert "feat: add feature" |
- `fix(api): resolve race condition in data sync`

content.user_title: Standardize Git Workflows and Pull Requests
content.value_statement: Inconsistent Git habits slow review and make history harder to understand. This skill guides worktrees, conventional commits, trailers, and pull requests for repeatable collaboration.
actual_capabilities: Explains when and how to use Git worktrees for parallel branch work.
Provides conventional commit formats, types, and message guidelines.
Shows how to add commit trailers for issues, reporters, and co-authors.
Supplies pull request title, description, test plan, and review checklist guidance.
Covers advanced Git tasks such as rebase, cherry-pick, stash, and bisect.
Lists common Git workflow mistakes and preferred team practices.
limitations: It is guidance only and does not inspect repository state by itself.
Commands may need changes for each project, branch policy, or hosting platform.
It does not replace team review rules, CI checks, or release approvals.
Destructive cleanup commands still require human confirmation before use.

use_cases.title: Plan Parallel Feature Work
use_cases.description: Create a clean worktree and branch naming plan for a new feature without disrupting current work.

use_cases.title: Prepare Reviewable Commits
use_cases.description: Turn a set of changes into conventional commits with clear subjects, bodies, and useful trailers.

use_cases.title: Standardize Pull Requests
use_cases.description: Draft a concise pull request title, description, test plan, and reviewer checklist.

prompt_templates.title: Choose a Worktree Name
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner setup for a new task
prompt_templates.prompt: Suggest a Git worktree name and branch type for this task: [describe the feature, bug fix, or experiment].

prompt_templates.title: Write a Commit Message
prompt_templates.prompt: Draft a conventional commit message for these changes. Include a short subject, a useful body, and any needed trailers.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare a Pull Request
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a pull request title, summary, change list, test plan, and related issues section from this change description.

prompt_templates.title: Clean Up Branch History
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this commit history and recommend which commits to squash, reword, or keep before opening a pull request.

output_examples.input: A developer needs to start an authentication feature while keeping current work untouched.
output: Cleanup note: remove the worktree only after the branch is merged and verified.

output_examples.input: A bug fix changes token refresh behavior and closes a reported issue.
output: Commit type: fix with auth scope.
Body should explain the expired-token behavior and user impact.
Trailer should reference the issue and reporter when available.

output_examples.input: A team wants a review-ready pull request for a small API change.
output: Use a conventional pull request title.
Summarize the behavior change in two short sentences.
List unit tests, integration tests, manual checks, and any breaking changes.

best_practices: Use one branch or worktree for each focused change.
Write commit messages that explain what changed and why.
Confirm cleanup commands before removing branches or worktrees.
anti_patterns: Do not mix unrelated fixes, features, and refactors in one pull request.
Do not leave vague commit messages such as fix bug or update.
Do not run forced cleanup commands against paths you have not verified.

faq.question: Does this skill run Git commands automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides guidance and examples. Any command execution depends on the calling tool and user approval policy.

faq.question: Can it help with conventional commits?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers commit types, scopes, subjects, bodies, and trailers for common development changes.

faq.question: Does it support Git worktrees?
faq.answer: Yes. It explains naming, setup, listing, pruning, and cleanup patterns for sibling worktrees.

faq.question: Can it create pull request descriptions?
faq.answer: Yes. It gives a practical structure for summaries, change lists, test plans, breaking changes, and related issues.

faq.question: Is this specific to GitHub?
faq.answer: Some examples mention GitHub issues, but the workflow can be adapted to most Git hosting systems.

faq.question: What should users verify before cleanup?
faq.answer: Users should confirm the repository, branch, target path, merge status, and whether local changes can be discarded.
